archetype.name: Pocket Passer (rhythm, intermediate-first)
archetype.definition: A big-armed starter now winning from the pocket with timing and ball placement, working short-to-intermediate windows at or just short of the sticks rather than living on scrambles or forced shots.

report.headline: Lawrence's accuracy leap looks real; the intermediate efficiency and red-zone luck won't hold.
report.take:
Lawrence has spent five seasons as a talented but uneven passer. Most years he was a volume producer whose accuracy hovered around average and whose interception totals ranked near the bottom of the league. Through five games of 2026 he looks like a different thrower. His CPOE of +7.65 ranks 2nd of 43 after back-to-back negative seasons, and his bad-throw rate of 7% ranks 5th of 36. Across his career that rate has run between roughly 14% and 20%. The offense around him leans slightly toward the run (pass rate over expected -1.7) and is backed by the league's 3rd-ranked defense. That keeps his volume modest: 143 attempts, 14th in yards. Per dropback he has been efficient: 0.274 EPA, 9th.

The engine is the middle of the field between 10 and 19 yards. On 41 intermediate throws he is producing 0.797 EPA a play with a 73% success rate and a CPOE of +17.2. Throws over the middle return 0.726 EPA. Jakobi Meyers (0.986 EPA per target) and Parker Washington (0.6 on a team-high 35 targets) are getting the ball in stride. This isn't a gunslinger story. His aggressiveness is 15.4% and he throws 1.49 yards short of the sticks on average. He is hitting windows on time and on target, and fewer bad throws explains much of the CPOE jump. That part can last. A 17-point CPOE on intermediate throws cannot.

The totals hide some soft spots. In the red zone he has 6 touchdowns on 26 attempts but is completing only 46.2%, with a CPOE of -3.7. The scoring rate there is outrunning the passing. On third down he converts just 36.8%, facing an average of 9.7 yards to go. In close fourth quarters his CPOE is -9 on 23 attempts. His legs have also gone quiet: 59 rushing yards and a 3.2% scramble rate, against 359 rushing yards last year. Sacks remain the tax. He is pressured on only 16.6% of dropbacks, 9th best, yet 32% of pressures become sacks, which ranks 28th of 36. He has run between 29% and 37.5% on that measure for three years, so this is who he is, not a new flaw. Two turnover-worthy fumbles with none lost is luck that won't always break his way.

His one bad game came at Denver, the 7th-ranked defense, where he posted -4.1 passing EPA and a 14.3% bad-throw rate. His best work came against the middle of the defensive rankings. Going forward, expect a quarterback who is genuinely more accurate than his career line. The efficiency should settle closer to 0.15-0.20 EPA per dropback as the intermediate numbers come back to earth. The touchdown rate on modest volume is the stat most likely to cool.

strengths.title: Ball placement has genuinely improved
strengths.body: His 7% bad-throw rate ranks 5th of 36, and his CPOE of +7.65 is 2nd of 43. Both are far better than anything on his career line, including a 13.9% bad-throw rate and -1.9 CPOE last season. Because it shows up in the charting, not just in completions, this reads as a real skill gain rather than a run of easy throws. Some of it will fade, but he should stay above his career baseline.

strengths.title: Owning the intermediate middle
strengths.body: The 10-19 yard band and the middle of the field are where his value lives: 0.797 EPA a play at intermediate depth and 0.726 over the middle. Meyers and Washington are winning there, and he is throwing on time with a 2.72-second release. The skill and the role are sustainable. A 73% success rate on 41 throws is not, and it will regress.

strengths.title: Explosive shots without forcing
strengths.body: He has 3 touchdowns and 1.02 EPA a play on just 14 deep attempts, with a CPOE of +13.4 on those throws. His aggressiveness sits at a measured 15.4%. Picking his spots this way works, though a 14-throw sample is a hint rather than proof.

concerns.title: Pressure still turns into sacks
concerns.body: He is rarely pressured, but 32% of pressures end in sacks, 28th of 36, and his sack rate of 6.5% ranks 22nd. That fits a career-long pattern: 29-37.5% pressure-to-sack in each of the last three years. He doesn't escape much anymore either, scrambling on only 3.2% of dropbacks. A line that already ranks 28th in hit rate allowed amplifies the problem, and this is the trait an aggressive pass rush can exploit.

concerns.title: Red-zone touchdowns outrunning the passing
concerns.body: He has 6 red-zone touchdowns while completing 46.2% there, with a negative CPOE and a 40.7% success rate. A 7% touchdown rate on 143 attempts is exactly the kind of number that regresses. Expect the touchdown pace to drift down even if the accuracy holds.

concerns.title: Third downs and late close games
concerns.body: He converts only 36.8% on third down, facing an average of 9.7 yards to go. That points partly to early-down failures, including the sacks. In close fourth quarters his completion rate falls to 47.8% with a -9 CPOE. Both are small samples, but they cut against the clean-efficiency narrative.

trend.note: Four of five games have been efficient. The Denver loss against a top-7 defense was the lone dud, and it was ugly. Week 5 brought his biggest volume (39 attempts, 331 yards) but his first negative-CPOE game, which hints the accuracy is starting to normalize.

nextGame.headline: A sack-heavy Houston front against a leaky secondary
nextGame.body:
Houston's defense is built to beat him in his weak spot. It ranks 3rd in sack rate and 8th in hit rate, and it is 4th in success rate allowed, so it wins a lot of downs. But when it loses, it loses big. It ranks 26th in explosive pass rate allowed and 26th in deep EPA allowed. Opposing WR1s have scored 6.5 PPR points a game over their averages against it, 30th of 32. Offenses also pass on Houston 4 points more than normal, the 5th-strongest pass funnel. The game turns on whether Lawrence gets the ball out before the rush arrives. If he does, his intermediate and deep shots fit what Houston gives up. If the protection leaks, his pressure-to-sack habit could produce another Denver.

Availability tilts both ways. Right tackle Anton Harrison (92% of snaps) left the London game with a knee injury and is questionable, which is a real worry against this pass rush. On Houston's side, safety Jalen Pitre (92% of snaps) is doubtful, which weakens a secondary already vulnerable deep. RB David Montgomery is also doubtful, which further limits a Houston run game that ranks 26th in rushing EPA. The forecast, five days out, shows 14 mph wind with gusts near 28. If that holds it would trim the deep game and the total, but it is too early to lean on.

keyMatchups.title: Houston pass rush vs. Jaguar protection
keyMatchups.body: Houston's 9% sack rate is 3rd in the league. Jacksonville allows hits at the 5th-highest rate, and Lawrence turns 32% of pressures into sacks. Harrison's status at right tackle is the swing piece. If he sits, expect multiple sacks and drive-killing long third downs.

keyMatchups.title: Shots against a vulnerable deep secondary
keyMatchups.body: Houston allows 0.915 EPA on deep throws, 26th, and is about to lose a 92%-snap safety in Pitre. Lawrence's 14 deep attempts have returned 1.02 EPA each. This is where his big plays should come from, wind permitting.

keyMatchups.title: Washington and the WR1 role
keyMatchups.body: Opposing WR1s run 6.5 PPR points a game over their averages against Houston, and 65.1% of the targets against it go to wideouts. The league share is 58%, while tight ends see only 17.4%. Expect the ball to tilt toward Washington and Meyers rather than Brenton Strange.

nextGame.watch: Whether Anton Harrison plays at right tackle, and how quickly Lawrence gets the ball out on early downs against Houston's rush.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy gain looks partly real. His bad-throw rate is a charting stat, and it has nearly halved from his career norm. That supports him finishing well above his career CPOE, but not at +7.65. The intermediate (0.797 EPA) and red-zone touchdown efficiency are the parts most likely to fade. Expect EPA per dropback to settle somewhere around 0.15-0.20, still top-12 territory. Touchdowns should come closer to 1.5-1.8 a game than 2.

Volume will stay capped by a run-leaning, defense-first team that is winning games. Sacks will remain the recurring drag unless the protection improves or he starts running again. His rushing has dropped to about 12 yards a game from roughly 21 last year, and that may come back some if he starts scrambling. His interception rate has been near the bottom of the league for most of his career. At 2.1% it is decent but ranks only 25th, so expect a pick most weeks.
swingFactors: Right tackle health and pass protection
How much of the intermediate accuracy holds
Whether the run-first, defense-led script persists

bets.reason: Four of Jacksonville's five games went under, with combined scores of 33-44. Their defense ranks 3rd in EPA and 3rd against the run. Houston's offense is 14th and 26th on the ground, and it will likely be without Montgomery. An early forecast of gusty wind would only push this lower.

Houston ranks 3rd in sack rate and 8th in hit rate. Jacksonville allows hits at the 5th-highest rate, and Lawrence turns 32% of pressures into sacks. His starting right tackle is questionable after leaving last game with a knee injury.

Jacksonville's defense ranks 3rd by EPA and 1st on short passes against a middling Houston offense missing its lead back. The Jaguars are 3-2 against the spread, and Houston's secondary is losing a 92%-snap safety. The low total and the pass-rush mismatch keep this a modest edge rather than a strong one.

confidence.note: Five games and 158 dropbacks. The accuracy gain has charting support, but the depth splits rest on small samples, and his right tackle is uncertain.
